claims.text: Replacing an EAM thermodynamic-integration reference with a dedicated neural-network interatomic potential will improve liquid-phase sampling in near-equimolar multicomponent alloys.
The neural-network reference will reduce free-energy path errors relative to EAM-based TOR-TILD references.
The proposed method applies to both solid and liquid near-equimolar high-entropy alloys at approximately 0.9–1.1 Tm.
The neural-network reference should be trained on a high-diversity set of first-principles snapshots of relevant liquid configurations.
The comparison should cover at least two quinary-or-higher high-entropy alloy compositions at ambient pressure and approximately 0.9–1.1 Tm.
Short-range chemical ordering occurs at high temperature in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
A liquid-trained neural-network reference will capture short-range order in multielement liquid configurations.
Capturing liquid short-range order will broaden phase-space overlap between the reference molecular dynamics and ab initio configurations.
EAM potentials have fixed functional forms that inadequately represent the relevant configurational diversity.
High-dimensional neural-network potentials can encode complex many-body interactions governing local structure in high-temperature alloy liquids.
Encoding these many-body interactions will reduce mismatch between reference and ab initio target thermodynamic paths.
The intervention is expected to improve thermodynamic-integration path consistency by a few meV per atom relative to EAM references.
Existing EAM-based TOR-TILD references for high-entropy alloys exhibit significant path deviations from ab initio data near melting.
The method is suitable for quinary-or-higher near-equimolar high-entropy alloys with melting points up to approximately 2000 K.
A sufficiently large and diverse ab initio training set is necessary for a robust neural-network reference potential.
The quantitative free-energy gain depends on training-set quality and compositional complexity.
Transferability outside the tested compositions and temperature window remains unvalidated.
Failure to improve over the EAM control, or free-energy deviations greater than a few meV per atom from ab initio results, would falsify the hypothesis.
